content.text: Enter QUINCE, SNUG, BOTTOM, FLUTE, SNOUT, and STARVELING

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Is all our company here?

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: You were best to call them generally, man by man,
according to the scrip.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Here is the scroll of every man's name, which is thought
fit, through all Athens, to play in our interlude before
the duke and the duchess, on his wedding-day at night.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: First, good Peter Quince, say what the play treats on,
then read the names of the actors, and so grow to a point.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Marry, our play is, The most lamentable comedy, and
most cruel death of Pyramus and Thisby.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: A very good piece of work, I assure you, and a merry.
Now, good Peter Quince, call forth your actors by the scroll.
Masters, spread yourselves.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Answer as I call you. Nick Bottom, the weaver.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: Ready. Name what part I am for, and proceed.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: You, Nick Bottom, are set down for Pyramus.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: What is Pyramus? a lover, or a tyrant?

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: A lover, that kills himself most gallant for love.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: That will ask some tears in the true performing of it:
if I do it, let the audience look to their eyes; I will
move storms, I will condole in some measure. To the rest:
yet my chief humour is for a tyrant: I could play
Ercles rarely, or a part to tear a cat in, to make all
split. The raging rocks
And shivering shocks
Shall break the locks
Of prison gates;
And Phibbus' car
Shall shine from far
And make and mar
The foolish Fates.
This was lofty! Now name the rest of the players. This is
Ercles' vein, a tyrant's vein; a lover is more condoling.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Francis Flute, the bellows-mender.

content.speaker: FLUTE
lines: Here, Peter Quince.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: You must take Thisby on you.

content.speaker: FLUTE
lines: What is Thisby? a wandering knight?

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: It is the lady that Pyramus must love.

content.speaker: FLUTE
lines: Nay, faith, let not me play a woman; I have a beard coming.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: That's all one: you shall play it in a mask, and you may
speak as small as you will.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: An I may hide my face, let me play Thisby too, I'll speak
in a monstrous little voice; 'Thisne, Thisne;' 'Ah,
Pyramus, my lover dear! thy Thisby dear, and lady dear!'

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: No, no; you must play Pyramus: and, Flute, you Thisby.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: Well, proceed.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Robin Starveling, the tailor.

content.speaker: STARVELING
lines: Here, Peter Quince.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Robin Starveling, you must play Thisby's mother. Tom Snout, the tinker.

content.speaker: SNOUT
lines: Here, Peter Quince.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: You, Pyramus' father: myself, Thisby's father: Snug, the joiner; you, the lion's part: and, I hope, here is a play fitted.

content.speaker: SNUG
lines: Have you the lion's part written? pray you, if it be, give it me, for I am slow of study.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: You may do it extempore, for it is nothing but roaring.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: Let me play the lion too: I will roar, that I will do any
man's heart good to hear me; I will roar, that I will
make the duke say 'Let him roar again, let him roar again.'

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: An you should do it too terribly, you would fright the
duchess and the ladies, that they would shriek; and that
were enough to hang us all.

content.speaker: ALL
lines: That would hang us, every mother's son.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: I grant you, friends, if that you should fright the ladies
out of their wits, they would have no more discretion but
to hang us: but I will aggravate my voice so that I will
roar you as gently as any sucking dove; I will roar you
an 'twere any nightingale.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: You can play no part but Pyramus; for Pyramus is a sweet-faced man; a proper man, as one shall see in a summer's day; a most lovely gentleman-like man: therefore you must needs play Pyramus.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: Well, I will undertake it. What beard were I best to play it in?

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Why, what you will.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: I will discharge it in either your straw-colour beard,
your orange-tawny beard, your purple-in-grain beard, or
your French-crown-colour beard, your perfect yellow.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: Some of your French crowns have no hair at all, and then
you will play barefaced. But, masters, here are your
parts: and I am to entreat you, request you and desire
you, to con them by to-morrow night; and meet me in the
palace wood, a mile without the town, by moonlight; there
will we rehearse, for if we meet in the city, we shall be
dogged with company, and our devices known. In the mean
time I will draw a bill of properties, such as our play
wants. I pray you, fail me not.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: We will meet; and there we may rehearse most obscenely and
courageously. Take pains; be perfect: adieu.

content.speaker: QUINCE
lines: At the duke's oak we meet.

content.speaker: BOTTOM
lines: Enough; hold or cut bow-strings.
